edges.description: Excitation-inhibition imbalance drives the seizure arm of the DEE mechanism.
The same molecular lesion independently disrupts circuit maturation, producing the developmental arm.
The hypersynchronous network state is what is observed clinically as the antiseizure-medication-refractory seizures that the ILAE operational definition puts at the centre of the DEE concept.

Status epilepticus is the failure of a seizure to self-terminate. Convulsive status epilepticus was recorded in 47 per cent and nonconvulsive status epilepticus in 19 per cent of a 510-patient genetic DEE cohort.
The same hypersynchrony is recorded interictally as frequent epileptiform activity on an abnormal EEG background, which is the electrographic rather than the clinical reading of this node.
Ongoing seizures and epileptiform activity themselves degrade cognitive and behavioural function.
Disrupted circuit maturation yields developmental delay and intellectual disability independently of seizure burden.

What this component adds is deterioration: worsening of development on a background of established impairment, rather than the delay itself. That is why loss of previously acquired skills is routed from here rather than from the developmental component, which the entry treats as the source of the delay.
Delayed acquisition of milestones is the direct expression of this component, and in the DEE concept it may precede seizure onset.
The cognitive endpoint of the developmental arm. Its features may persist despite adequate seizure control, which is the clinical observation that makes this arm separable from the epileptic one.

Autistic features are routed from the developmental rather than the epileptic arm because they are part of the cognitive and behavioural phenotype of the underlying genetic lesion. The sources cited here name autism spectrum disorder and behavioural deficits as features of the DEE group without attributing them to either arm, so the routing is this entry's model rather than a claim either source makes.

Movement disorders are routed from the developmental arm because most of the epilepsy-dyskinesia genes map to the same ion-channel and synaptic pathways as the upstream lesion nodes, rather than arising from the seizure burden. The cited review reports co-occurrence and gene-pathway membership; it does not test which arm produces the movement disorder, so this edge is an inference from the entry's two-component model.

A lesion in metabolic, transport, proteostasis, RNA-processing, cytoskeletal or genome-maintenance machinery disrupts circuit maturation directly, producing the developmental arm without requiring a primary change in channel conduction.

The same non-channel lesions also reach excitation-inhibition balance, either by limiting the supply of neurotransmitter precursors and the ion gradients that neuronal firing depends on, or by altering neuronal excitability directly.
Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy accounted for 19 of 42 deaths in a 510-patient genetic DEE cohort, so ongoing seizures are a proximate route from this phenotype to premature death.

nodes.description: A large share of the genes in which pathogenic variants cause genetic DEE encode neither an ion channel nor a core synaptic protein, and the DEE literature explicitly separates these mechanisms from the channelopathies. The gene-defined subtypes wired at this node in this entry span Rac-GEF-dependent neuronal polarity (DOCK7), actin and protein-phosphatase-1 regulation in cortical migration (PHACTR1), receptor tyrosine kinase signalling (NTRK2), spliceosomal small nuclear RNA (RNU2-2), de-UFMylation (UFSP2), endoplasmic-reticulum stress signalling (RNF13), mitochondrial protein biosynthesis and mitochondrial trafficking (PARS2, TRAK1), purine metabolism and asparagine-linked glycosylation (ITPA, ALG13), endolysosomal acidification (ATP6V0A1), Na+/K+-ATPase pump function and neutral amino-acid transport (ATP1A2, SLC38A3), DNA repair (PNKP), and one gene in the 1q41-q42 microdeletion interval whose molecular function no reference cited here states (FBXO28). The DEE-series subtypes added under this parent extend that list with a Krebs cycle enzyme (MDH2), an endoplasmic-reticulum co-chaperone (CNPY3), a cut homeodomain transcription factor (CUX2), a cohesin subunit (SMC1A), a factor that targets arginine tRNAs for 3-methylcytosine modification (DALRD3), the v-ATPase A subunit (ATP6V1A), a nucleocytoplasmic shuttling RNA-binding protein (CELF2), a trans-Golgi network protein required for peptide hormone processing (HID1), a microtubule-associated serine-threonine kinase (MAST3), an inhibitory component of the mTOR pathway (DEPDC5), the anaphase-promoting complex subunit Cdh1 (FZR1), an ESCRT-II subunit (SNF8), the BRCA1-associated ATM activator (BRAT1), and the neuron-specific beta subunit of the AP-3 vesicle coat adaptor (AP3B2). AP3B2 is placed here rather than at the synaptic node because the AP-3 complex acts in organelle and vesicle biogenesis rather than at the synapse itself. Each functional assignment is taken from the publication cited on that subtype's own has_subtypes row. The node is kept separate from the ion-channel and synaptic lesion node because the two classes reach the shared excitation-inhibition and neurodevelopmental arms by different routes, not because the subtypes here are milder.

nodes.description:
A de novo or inherited pathogenic variant in one of a large and growing set of genes encoding voltage-gated ion channels (e.g. SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, KCNQ2, KCNA2, KCNT1, CACNA1E, HCN1), presynaptic vesicle-cycle and neurotransmitter-release machinery (STXBP1, DNM1, SNAP25, CPLX1, UNC13A), postsynaptic glutamate or GABA receptors (GRIN1, GRIN2A, GRIN2B, GABRA1, GABRB3), or chromatin/transcriptional regulators active in neurodevelopment (CDKL5, FOXG1, CHD2) disrupts normal neuronal excitability or synaptic signaling.
Gene-defined subtypes wired at this node in this entry, beyond the examples above, are CACNA2D1 (the alpha-2-delta-1 auxiliary subunit of CaV1 and CaV2 voltage-gated calcium channels), FGF13/FHF2 (an intracellular regulator of voltage-gated sodium channels), SV2A (a synaptic vesicle glycoprotein and the binding site of levetiracetam), FRRS1L (an AMPA receptor outer-core protein), LGI1 together with its postsynaptic receptor ADAM22, BAIAP2 (dendritic spine morphogenesis and excitatory synapse formation), and ACTL6B (a subunit of the neuron-specific chromatin remodelling complex nBAF). Each functional assignment is taken from the publication cited on that subtype's own has_subtypes row.
The DEE-series subtypes added under this parent extend that list with four further voltage-gated channel subunits (SCN3A/Nav1.3, KCNC2/Kv3.2, KCNH5/EAG2-Kv10.2, and the sodium-activated potassium channel KCNT2); the stretch-activated channel TMEM63B; four GABA receptor subunits, namely the GABA-A subunits GABRB2, GABRA2 and GABRA5 together with the metabotropic GABA-B subunit GABBR2; the vesicular GABA transporter SLC32A1; and three further components of the presynaptic vesicle cycle, namely the AAA ATPase NSF, which acts in SNARE complex assembly and disassembly, its beta attachment protein NAPB, and the polyphosphoinositide phosphatase SYNJ1.

evidence.snippet: KCNQ2, CDKL5, SCN1A, and STXBP1 were the most frequently identified genes.

evidence.reference_title: National survey on the prevalence of single-gene aetiologies for genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathies in Italy.
evidence.snippet: The most frequently reported genes in the survey were SCN1A (16%), followed by KCNQ2 (5.6%) and SCN2A (5%).

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in SCN3A cause early infantile epileptic encephalopathy.
evidence.snippet: Here, we describe a cohort of 4 patients with epileptic encephalopathy and heterozygous de novo missense variants in SCN3A (p.Ile875Thr in 2 cases, p.Pro1333Leu, and p.Val1769Ala).

evidence.reference_title: Rates of Status Epilepticus and Sudden Unexplained Death in Epilepsy in People With Genetic Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathies.
evidence.snippet: Four genes were associated with SUDEP: SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, and STXBP1.

evidence.reference_title: De Novo Missense Variants in SLC32A1 Cause a Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy Due to Impaired GABAergic Neurotransmission.
evidence.snippet: Using exome sequencing, we identified four individuals with a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy and de novo missense variants in SLC32A1.

evidence.reference_title: Biallelic variants in SLC38A3 encoding a glutamine transporter cause epileptic encephalopathy.
evidence.snippet: Our data support the contention that SLC38A3 is a novel disease gene for developmental and epileptic encephalopathy and illuminate the likely pathophysiology of the disease as perturbations in glutamine homeostasis.

evidence.reference_title: Heterozygous truncation mutations of the SMC1A gene cause a severe early onset epilepsy with cluster seizures in females: Detailed phenotyping of 10 new cases.
evidence.snippet: Ten cases with heterozygous de novo mutations in the SMC1A gene are presented. All 10 mutations identified are predicted to result in premature truncation of the SMC1A protein.

evidence.reference_title: Bi-allelic variants in SNF8 cause a disease spectrum ranging from severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy to syndromic optic atrophy.
evidence.snippet: We report nine individuals from six families presenting with a spectrum of neurodevelopmental/neurodegenerative features caused by bi-allelic variants in SNF8 (GenBank: NM_007241.4), encoding the ESCRT-II subunit SNF8.

evidence.reference_title: Exome sequencing for patients with developmental and epileptic encephalopathies in clinical practice.
evidence.snippet: KCNQ2, CDKL5, SCN1A, and STXBP1 were the most frequently identified genes.

evidence.reference_title: Homozygous Mutation in Synaptic Vesicle Glycoprotein 2A Gene Results in Intractable Epilepsy, Involuntary Movements, Microcephaly, and Developmental and Growth Retardation.
evidence.snippet: Levetiracetam, which binds to SV2A, was not effective as an antiepileptic medication.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of SYNJ1 dual phosphatase activity leads to early onset refractory seizures and progressive neurological decline.
evidence.snippet: We performed whole exome or genome sequencing in three independent sib pairs with early onset refractory seizures and progressive neurological decline, and identified novel segregating recessive SYNJ1 defects.

nodes.description: Convulsive and nonconvulsive status epilepticus are frequent and life-threatening complications, affecting roughly half and one fifth of patients respectively across genetic DEE cohorts, with the highest burden in SCN1A-related disease.

evidence.reference_title: Rates of Status Epilepticus and Sudden Unexplained Death in Epilepsy in People With Genetic Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathies.
evidence.snippet: The cohort comprised 510 individuals with a genetic DEE, in whom we observed CSE in 47% and NCSE in 19%.

evidence.reference_title: Rates of Status Epilepticus and Sudden Unexplained Death in Epilepsy in People With Genetic Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathies.
evidence.snippet: The highest proportion of CSE occurred in patients with SCN1A-associated DEEs, including 181/203 (89%; 95% CI 84-93) patients with Dravet syndrome

nodes.description: Approved as adjunctive therapy for Dravet syndrome in combination with clobazam, where a randomised controlled trial demonstrated clear efficacy. CHEBI has no stiripentol term, so the agent is bound to NCIT following the documented NCIT-fallback convention for drugs lacking a CHEBI entry.

evidence.reference_title: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies.
evidence.snippet: In Dravet syndrome, a RCT of stiripentol demonstrated clear efficacy

evidence.reference_title: Stretch-activated ion channel TMEM63B associates with developmental and epileptic encephalopathies and progressive neurodegeneration.
evidence.snippet: Here, we describe 17 unrelated individuals with severe early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), intellectual disability, and severe motor and cortical visual impairment associated with progressive neurodegenerative brain changes carrying ten distinct heterozygous variants of TMEM63B, encoding for a highly conserved stretch-activated ion channel.

evidence.reference_title: Deleterious variants in TRAK1 disrupt mitochondrial movement and cause fatal encephalopathy.
evidence.snippet: This study confirms the role of TRAK1 in mitochondrial dynamics and constitutes the first report of this gene in association with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder.

evidence.reference_title: A pathogenic UFSP2 variant in an autosomal recessive form of pediatric neurodevelopmental anomalies and epilepsy.
evidence.snippet: Different UFSP2 variants cause markedly different diseases, with homozygosity for V115E causing a severe syndrome of neurodevelopmental disability and epilepsy.
